$comment: Recorded results a CI run is compared against. Update it only together with the skill or the eval set, in the same PR, the way a snapshot test is updated — never to make a red run go green.

runs.reading: Saturated. An agent with the repo derives these rules from server/.dependency-cruiser.cjs and AGENTS.md.

Also saturated: v1.0.0 reached every mechanism by reading the depcruise config itself. Case 4 turned out not to be a blind spot at all — service-stays-http-agnostic does catch a type-only import under tsPreCompilationDeps.

runs.id: secret-cache (case 6), v1.1.0 vs v1.0.0, 5 runs per side
runs.reading: Unanimous on both sides — no assertion split, so detection is not fragile either way. The 3-vs-0 false-finding gap is p≈0.17: a hypothesis, not a result. What five runs did establish: v1.1.0's token spread is five times tighter (±1.8k vs ±8.5k).

runs.id: team-conventions (case 7), v2.0.0 vs v1.1.0, 5 runs per side
runs.reading: The first real delta. Three discriminating assertions split 5/5 vs 0/5 (Fisher p≈0.008 each) while all controls stayed 25/25 — a targeted blind spot, not a weaker reviewer. Baseline reframed the widened `reviews` table as a cross-module write (different fix, columns stay) and, on cascades, three of five actively recommended new ON DELETE CASCADE.

gate.$comment: Absolute, not relative. On cases 0-6 the delta is 0, so a 'must beat baseline' gate would fail on a healthy skill; case 7 is the only one where the delta itself is meaningful, and one case is too thin to gate on. This gate answers the question CI can answer: did an edit to the skill make it worse. 0.9 leaves room for one missed assertion — a single model run is noisy.

onion-architecture.known_weakness: Cases 0-6 are saturated: both configurations score 100%, so they are regression guards, not A/B instruments. Only case 7 (group `team-decisions`) discriminates, and it does so because its rules are not recoverable from any file in the repo. See .claude/skills/onion-architecture/evals/README.md.
